bundle.prompt:
Below is a passage from a college course, the course plan for its chapter (objectives and concepts, by id), and the plan items the passage is declared to teach.
For each declared item, say whether the passage teaches or practises it ("yes"), touches it only in passing ("passing"), or does not deal with it ("no").
If the passage teaches an item of the plan it is not declared for, name its id. If it teaches nothing in the plan at all, say so.
Judge what the passage does for a student, not its wording or quality.
Reply with JSON only, exactly this shape: {"nonce": "8e130ef2328d64ba", "links": [{"id": "...", "verdict": "yes" | "passing" | "no", "why": "..."}], "also": ["<id>"], "offPlan": false}

THE CHAPTER'S PLAN
- objective.chemical-equilibrium.define-equilibrium: Define chemical equilibrium as a dynamic state in which the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and the concentrations no longer change.
- objective.chemical-equilibrium.write-k-expression: Write the equilibrium constant expression for a given balanced reaction, placing the products in the numerator and raising each concentration to its stoichiometric coefficient.
- objective.chemical-equilibrium.compare-q-and-k: Evaluate the reaction quotient and compare it to the equilibrium constant to predict which direction the reaction will shift.
- objective.chemical-equilibrium.omit-pure-phases: Explain why pure solids and pure liquids, whose activity is taken as one, are omitted from the equilibrium constant expression.
- objective.chemical-equilibrium.relate-k-to-gibbs: Relate the equilibrium constant to the standard Gibbs energy change using ΔG° = −RT ln K.
- objective.chemical-equilibrium.predict-k-with-temperature: Predict how a change in temperature changes the equilibrium constant using the sign of the reaction enthalpy (the van 't Hoff relation).
- concept.chemical-equilibrium.equal-rates: At chemical equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal, nonzero rates, so the reactant and product concentrations no longer change with time.
- concept.chemical-equilibrium.dynamic-exchange: Equilibrium is dynamic: individual molecules keep reacting in both directions even though the macroscopic concentrations stay constant.
- concept.chemical-equilibrium.k-expression: For a balanced reaction αA + βB ⇌ σS + τT, the equilibrium constant equals the product concentrations divided by the reactant concentrations, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient, with the products written in the numerator.
- concept.chemical-equilibrium.pure-phases-omitted: Pure solids and pure liquids have an activity of one and therefore do not appear in the equilibrium constant expression.
- concept.chemical-equilibrium.reaction-quotient: The reaction quotient has the same form as the equilibrium constant but is evaluated at any composition, and comparing it to the equilibrium constant tells which direction the reaction will shift.
- concept.chemical-equilibrium.k-and-gibbs: The equilibrium constant is related to the standard Gibbs energy change of the reaction by ΔG° = −RT ln K.
- concept.chemical-equilibrium.k-depends-on-temperature: The equilibrium constant depends on temperature through the van 't Hoff equation: raising the temperature increases the equilibrium constant for an endothermic reaction and decreases it for an exothermic reaction.
- concept.chemical-equilibrium.catalyst-no-shift: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor and therefore changes neither the equilibrium constant nor the position of equilibrium.
- misconception.chemical-equilibrium.reactions-stopped: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions have stopped and nothing is happening at the molecular level.
- misconception.chemical-equilibrium.concentrations-equal: At equilibrium the concentrations of reactants and products are equal to each other.
- misconception.chemical-equilibrium.catalyst-shifts-yield: Adding a catalyst shifts the equilibrium toward the products and increases the yield.
- misconception.chemical-equilibrium.solid-changes-k: Adding more of a pure solid or pure liquid changes the value of the equilibrium constant.
- misconception.chemical-equilibrium.concentration-changes-k: Changing the concentrations of the species changes the value of the equilibrium constant (rather than only temperature changing it).
- concept.course.dynamic-equilibrium: A reversible reaction reaches a dynamic equilibrium where the forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal, nonzero rates.
- concept.course.equilibrium-constant: The equilibrium constant quantifies the balance of products to reactants once a reaction has reached equilibrium.
- concept.course.q-versus-k: Comparing the reaction quotient to the equilibrium constant predicts the direction in which a reaction not yet at equilibrium will move.
- concept.course.le-chatelier-principle: Le Chatelier's principle predicts qualitatively how an equilibrium already reached shifts to partially counteract a disturbance.
- concept.course.temperature-changes-k: A temperature change both shifts the equilibrium position and changes the value of the equilibrium constant, whereas concentration, volume, and pressure changes shift the position without changing the equilibrium constant.

DECLARED ITEMS
- objective.chemical-equilibrium.write-k-expression

TEXT BEFORE THE PASSAGE (context only)
Write the equilibrium constant expression for $\ce{2 SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2 SO3(g)}$, then write it
for the same reaction written in reverse. How are the two related? *(Objective 2)*

PASSAGE (Answer 4)
Forward: $K = \dfrac{[\ce{SO3}]^{2}}{[\ce{SO2}]^{2}[\ce{O2}]}$.

Reverse: $K' = \dfrac{[\ce{SO2}]^{2}[\ce{O2}]}{[\ce{SO3}]^{2}}$.

The two are reciprocals: $K' = 1/K$. Reversing the equation swaps numerator and denominator.
